name: Sleep banking
lead: Sleep banking, also called sleep extension, is the practice of sleeping more than usual in the days before an expected period of sleep loss, in the hope of reducing later impairment. It is discussed in military, shift-work and medical contexts and in some self-improvement circles.

Research is limited. A 2025 commentary in the journal Sleep debated whether banking produces a surplus of sleep-dependent brain resources,[1] and a 2026 narrative review examined its role in reducing cognitive and motor impairment from later sleep restriction.[2] Sleep medicine bodies cited on Wikipedia say the only sure way to counter sleep deprivation is more nightly sleep.[3]

paras: The idea is to build up a reserve before a planned sleep-restricted period such as military operations, night shifts or long duty hours. Military reviews note that increasing nightly sleep time is the main method of counteracting sleep deprivation but is often not feasible during operations.[4][5]

Mathematical models of performance under chronic sleep restriction and total sleep deprivation have been developed to predict impairment.[6] A study of resident physicians examined sleep strategies for improving night-shift performance.[7] Sleep-medicine texts recommend at least seven hours nightly for adults.[8]

Human studies of banking exist in small numbers and are summarized in a 2026 narrative review on reducing cognitive and motor impairments from later restriction.[2] A 2025 paper debates whether it creates a surplus of sleep-dependent brain resources.[1] No studies found on sleep banking and facial appearance.

card.summary: Sleeping extra ahead of planned sleep loss: studied in military and shift-work settings, with unsettled evidence.
card.note: Researchers still debate whether a sleep surplus can be stored.

quick.overview:
Sleep banking means sleeping extra before an expected stretch of poor sleep.

Military and shift-work researchers study it, and recent reviews describe the evidence as still developing.
quick.mechanism: Believers say extra sleep builds a reserve that cushions later impairment; researchers are debating whether sleep-dependent brain resources can be stored.[1][2]
quick.risks: No specific harms are described in the sources reviewed. Sleep guidance cited recommends at least seven hours nightly for adults.[8]
